title: Built to Last
author: Jim Collins and Jerry I. Porras
theme: Enduring great companies hold a fixed core ideology while relentlessly stimulating change and progress in everything else.
summary: Jim Collins and Jerry Porras spent six years studying what they called visionary companies: firms that had led their industries for generations and were widely admired. They paired each one with a solid but less outstanding rival from the same era and industry, such as Merck with Pfizer or Hewlett-Packard with Texas Instruments, and asked what truly separated them. Over many decades the visionary group delivered stock returns far above both its rivals and the general market.

Their first finding overturns several myths. These companies seldom began with a brilliant product idea, and they did not depend on charismatic, larger-than-life leaders. Their founders were more like clock builders than time tellers: instead of personally announcing the right answer, they designed organisations that could keep producing good answers long after they had gone.

At the centre of each enduring company sits a core ideology, made up of a few deeply held values and a purpose that goes beyond making money. Profit matters, but it is treated like oxygen, needed for life rather than being the point of life. The specific values differ from firm to firm; what counts is that they are authentic and consistently honoured.

The second half of the formula is a restless drive for progress. Visionary companies set bold, long-range goals that energise people, keep experimenting and retain what works, and refuse to treat any level of performance as good enough.

To protect the core, they build strong, almost cult-like cultures that suit believers and push out those who do not fit. They also tend to grow leaders from within rather than hiring outside saviours, which keeps the ideology intact across generations.

The authors urge managers to reject the tyranny of choosing either stability or change. Great companies embrace both, preserving their core while changing practices, and they align every system, policy and incentive so that the ideology is lived, not merely written down.
takeaway: Build an organisation, not a personality: anchor it in timeless values and purpose, then change everything else boldly and continuously.

questions.q: How did Collins and Porras design their research?
options: By surveying thousands of small start-ups
By comparing visionary companies with solid rivals from the same industry and era
By interviewing only current chief executives about their plans
By ranking firms purely on one year of profits
questions.why: Each visionary company was paired with a good but less outstanding competitor so the differences between them could be identified.

questions.q: What does the 'clock building, not time telling' idea mean?
options: Leaders should focus on meeting every deadline
Companies should invest in precise scheduling systems
Founders should create organisations that keep succeeding without depending on them
Managers should forecast markets more accurately
questions.why: A clock builder creates a lasting mechanism, whereas a time teller relies on personal brilliance that ends when they leave.

questions.q: Which belief did the study find to be a myth?
options: Visionary companies need a great idea to get started
Visionary companies have a core ideology
Visionary companies develop leaders internally
Visionary companies keep pushing for progress
questions.why: Many visionary companies started without a brilliant product idea and found their way through trial and adaptation.

questions.q: What two elements make up a company's core ideology in the book?
options: Market share and growth rate
Brand and pricing
Strategy and structure
Core values and a purpose beyond making money
questions.why: The authors define core ideology as enduring values plus a fundamental reason for existing that goes beyond profit.

questions.q: How do visionary companies view profit, according to the authors?
options: As the only goal that matters
As necessary for survival but not the ultimate purpose
As something to avoid discussing
As less important than market share
questions.why: Profit is compared to oxygen: essential for life, but not the reason the company exists.

options: A bold, long-range goal that energises and unites people
A budgeting method for annual planning
A personality test used in hiring
A type of performance bonus
questions.why: A Big Hairy Audacious Goal is a clear, compelling and ambitious target that stimulates progress.

questions.q: What do the authors mean by the 'Genius of the AND'?
options: Hiring both specialists and generalists
Combining two companies through a merger
Embracing apparent opposites, such as stability and change, at the same time
Using two different accounting systems
questions.why: Visionary companies refuse forced either-or choices and pursue seemingly contradictory goals together.

questions.q: Why do visionary companies have 'cult-like' cultures?
options: To keep salaries low
To avoid government regulation
To make the company secretive about its products
To preserve the core ideology by fitting in believers and filtering out those who do not share it
questions.why: A strong, demanding culture protects the core values so that the ideology survives over time.

questions.q: Where do visionary companies usually find their top leaders?
options: From famous outside executives
From within the company
From consulting firms
From the board of directors
questions.why: Home-grown leaders understand and carry the core ideology, ensuring continuity across generations.

questions.q: What does 'try a lot of stuff and keep what works' describe?
options: Random hiring practices
Cutting costs across all departments
Evolutionary progress through experimentation and selection
Outsourcing all research
questions.why: Many visionary companies advanced by running many small experiments and building on the ones that succeeded.
